nameStory: The White-faced Ibis gets its name from the distinctive white border that frames its face during breeding season, creating a striking mask-like appearance. This white facial outline makes it easy to distinguish from its close cousin, the Glossy Ibis, which lacks this telltale marking.
description: The White-faced Ibis is a large wading bird with a long, curved bill perfect for probing muddy wetlands for food. These chocolate-brown birds with glossy, iridescent feathers stand about two feet tall with long legs built for wading through shallow water. During breeding season, they develop the characteristic white face outline that gives them their name, along with bright red eyes and legs.

idTips.label: White facial border
idTips.description: During breeding season, look for a thin white line that outlines the face like a delicate mask - this is the key field mark that separates it from other ibises

idTips.label: Curved bill
idTips.description: Long, thin bill that curves downward like a sickle - perfect for feeling around in mud for crayfish, worms, and insects

idTips.label: Glossy plumage
idTips.description: Rich chestnut-brown body with an oily, metallic sheen that shows hints of purple and green in good light - feels smooth and sleek if you ever handle a museum specimen

idTips.label: Red eyes and legs
idTips.description: Bright red or orange-red eyes and legs during breeding season that almost seem to glow - a stark contrast to the dark plumage

idTips.label: Colonial behavior
idTips.description: Often feeds in small flocks, walking slowly through shallow water with heads down, methodically probing the bottom

habitat: In New England, White-faced Ibis are rare visitors to freshwater and brackish marshes, flooded fields, and shallow pond edges. They prefer areas with soft, muddy bottoms where they can easily probe for aquatic invertebrates, often associating with other wading birds like herons and egrets.

seasonality.spring: Rare spring migrants may appear in May, often showing the beginning of white facial markings and reddening eyes and legs.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time if present - full breeding plumage with bright white face border, red eyes and legs makes identification straightforward.
seasonality.fall: Occasional fall visitors lack the white face markings, making identification much more challenging and requiring careful comparison with Glossy Ibis.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England during winter months, as most birds migrate to warmer southern regions.

funFact: White-faced Ibis have specialized nerve endings in their bill tips that work like underwater fingers, allowing them to feel and identify prey in murky water without seeing it - they can literally taste-test a potential meal before deciding whether to swallow it!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with the more common Glossy Ibis, especially outside breeding season when both species look nearly identical. Memory trick: 'White-faced = white lace around the face' - if you don't see that delicate white outline during breeding season, it's probably a Glossy Ibis.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'White-faced,' this bird only shows the white facial markings during breeding season - for much of the year it looks remarkably similar to other dark ibises, which explains why many sightings go unconfirmed outside of breeding months.
compareHints: White-faced Ibis differs from Glossy Ibis primarily by the white facial border during breeding season and slightly different bill and leg coloration. The white face outline is paper-thin but distinctive, while Glossy Ibis maintains dark facial skin year-round with no contrasting border.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While the similar White-faced Ibis occasionally appears in New England, Glossy Ibis lacks the distinctive white border around the face and red eyes that characterize its western cousin.
